en: Who were those who inhabited Talas,
Where many khans came to plunder
Yet could not crush and defeat its men?
They never yielded their place to another;
You are the descendants of those keen-edged lions—
If hostile death comes, fly into the bullets!
Plunge the accursed enemy’s head
Into the turmoil of battle;
If your strength begins to fail,
Split open his black liver
And lie face-down upon the earth.
If your power and strength prevail,
Give the devouring son of the ogre
The punishment he deserves!
My sons, do not remain alive—
Die by Sarybai’s hand!
How could we heed the words
Of the ogre’s swine of a son
Because he is said to be a wrathful champion?
How can we, the honorable ancestral Kyrgyz people,
While our dear heads still live,
Hand the nation over to him?
If hostile death comes, then die;
For the vast common people,
See once more, my sons,
The true path from which there is no retreat.
In this wretched world of meager fortune,
Does one who fears death ever prosper?
Has there ever been one born
With an iron core who neither dies nor perishes?
In this false and miserable world,
This speaking tongue will be stilled,
The span of worldly life will contract;
When the angel stretches out five fingers,
When the angel who takes life
Draws near,
What soul can flee and escape
The death that has been written?
The dug grave receives us;
Beneath it lies the vast black earth
That has reaped the whole wide world—
None of us is immortal.
If our wretched heads are destined for death,
If we are buried beneath the ground,
The earth is the millstone, and we are peas.
The army surged in a seething mass,
Let the fine muskets fire fiercely.
Those whose hour has come, whose days are done,
Let them swiftly meet their death,
That the Kyrgyz cause may prosper,
And Sarybai, not a hair left of him,
May vanish from this world.
May broad Talas, left by our fathers,
Remain an inheritance to their descendants,
And dwelling in the Ala-Too,
May the noble Kyrgyz be a nation.
May Sarybai, who has set his enmity upon us,
Perish and become black earth!
Let blood be shed and people die;
All you people who fight Sarybai,
This infidel son of a monster,
Make the tyrant bleed,
Lay all his people low,
To the delight of our bitter enemy,
He has ravaged those with royal camps,
This swine, the monster’s son,
This infidel who has brought down doom,
This cruel and calamitous warrior,
Has made it known to all the people,
Abandoning broad Talas for the Ala-Too,
He has laid waste to all the land,
Slain every leader,
And brought the dear people to ruin.
How can we stand and watch
One ravaging dog become khan?
How can we go on living?
If the raging Sarybai
Should suddenly seize you in his hands,
If you are caught in his iron net,
If you fall into his pit,
If you yourself are snared in disaster—
His heart is foul, his nature mean;
Few such creatures are ever born.
He will leave your locks shorn in mourning,
So, Kyrgyz who ride straight against him,
Show your keenest valor,
Against the imperious foe Sarybai,
Who rains down fire and stones;
Upon that accursed incendiary himself,
Bring death and calamity!
Break his despotic power;
You are sons of the sovereign Kyrgyz—
Extinguish him like a fire!
How can we submit to the tyranny
Of the infidel monster’s son?
How can we, undying yet unavenged, live in shame,
And let the ancestral Kyrgyz land
Become another’s spoil?
Whatever Sarybai may say,
He is fierce in spirit, a great calamity;
How can we submit to his rule?
If we make Sarybai khan,
Let him devastate and slaughter the people,
What inheritance shall we ever gain?
It seems this swine longs
To leave not a hair of the Kyrgyz—
Then let us perish in battle!
Rather than let Sarybai reign supreme,
Rather than let the swine master the Kyrgyz,
What good is it to stir and linger?
Let every Kyrgyz, not a hair remaining,
Perish in slaughter
At the oppressor’s hands.
Let every hillside turn to dust,
Let every hollow fill with blood,
Let every slope be veiled in dust,
Let armies gather with a roar!
Let the black earth tremble,
Let these people wade in blood.
Let war cries swell into a din;
Here is the place of combat—
Let the tumult split the sky!
Let the earth crack and part,
Let the doomed shed their blood,
Let dust fly up to heaven,
Scatter his blood like water.
Mighty Kyrgyz, you are our wings;
To strike down a charging foe
Is the custom left by your forefathers.
From time beyond remembering,
When has this strife ever ceased?
Since the earth was made and peoples arose,
Since our tribe became Kyrgyz,
There has been no reckoning of the dead.
We suffered humiliation and gathered again;
Harried and scattered by the enemy,
We were oppressed for seven generations.
First we were in Altai,
Many were scattered to Kanghai,
Many of us went away to Eren,
For our persecuting enemies were many;
Many Kyrgyz descended
Into depths from which none returned.
Because of cruel enemies,
At times we scattered,
Beyond the land of El-Körbös;
At times we Kyrgyz went
Among the people of Hindustan.
Blood was shed in combat;
From age to age,
From time to time,
We Kyrgyz suffered mighty oppression
And were divided by the measure of the lash.
Despite enemies who dealt us wrath,
Our precious lives still appeared alive.
When hostile enemies came,
We clashed and battled;
Blood was shed and warriors died,
But the formidable, blessed Kyrgyz people
Never failed to take revenge,
For honor and for the people.
Their heroes died.”
So spoke the brave gray wolf,
The princely son of Manas,
Stirring a great commotion throughout the world.
He makes us slaves lower than beasts.
He lets us sow no crops,
He lets us camp nowhere freely,
He lets us tether not even two mares.
He will unleash his wrath upon the multitude,
Reduce this land to less than a hair,
And mercilessly slaughter these people.
With brave Seytek and Külchoro
Proclaimed the leaders of the people,
What inheritance shall we gain?
Let us spare not a single life
And perish fighting;
O wretched Kyrgyz people,
Let us pass away as sacrifices.
When the khan dies, let the people die;
Let the whole multitude die!
Once the head that leads is gone,
Once you die and your days are done,
Let the eyes of this fallen head close in peace,
So that the multitude left behind
May see days of happiness!
The wrathful Sarybai
Is a flood that will engulf us,
A black and blazing fire,
A deadly bullet from a matchlock;
His breath burns the soul,
He is an ember huge as Mount Kap.
O lion-born descendants of the Kyrgyz,
Turn aside in every direction
The raging flood he drives upon us!
Stand tall and bare your breasts
Before death’s bullets;
O dear people, vast as lake and river,
Summon the strength to quench
His red embers, huge as Mount Kap.
Advance and extinguish the fire;
That swine who seeks to rule,
Bind him by a hair
And cast him down.
Do not make Sarybai a giant,
Let us bind him by a hair and cast him down.
Do not make Sarybai a giant,
Do not let him rule this Talas;
Let our blood flow like water,
Let us all perish!
Rather than be ambushed from the heights,
And have every valiant lion
Delivered into Sarybai’s hands,
Rather than lose mane and tail
And wander stripped and forlorn,
Rather than live with broken horns,
Polled and powerless,
Calling Sarybai our lord,
And burning in anguish,
Let us flee Talas in terror,
And, fighting seven years without cease,
Ransack every last saddlebag
Of the infidel monster’s son.
Let the multitude begin the battle;
Old men bent low and growing youths alike,
Let us abandon everything,
And rise in open strife
Against the oppressor.
Without delay, level your spears;
Let us wage a furious battle.
Brave Semetey, Külchoro,
And brave Seytek, whom we make our hope—
Let the whole people take these three
As the girdle around their waists.
Against the tyrant’s forces,
Let us stand in bitter battle.
If Sarybai is truly a hero,
Let us perish in slaughter.
The people surge like a river;
When the river floods and torrents run,
We shall see what Sarybai is worth—
Let us grapple with that dog!”
The people cried out in tumult,
In a roar that split the heavens;
Horns and trumpets sounded,
Warriors spoke and the people grew impassioned,
Voicing countless words.
Brave young men and thoroughbred steeds,
All together grew impassioned.
Wisdom took the lead;
Not only their livestock but their lives
The multitude renounced, saying,
“The hero’s words are true.”
“How can anyone say we shall not face
Cannon fire and turmoil?
If hostile death has reached us,
